text: Kinetic energy. It's plausible to suppose that a larger velocity of a body will have a greater effect on other bodies. This does not depend on the direction of the velocity, only its magnitude, that is speed. The larger effect can be translated into a larger potential to do work once the fast moving body strikes a slower one. An example is through billiards or pool when the fast moving white cue ball strikes the blue-colored tube ball. The faster the cue, the more the tube ball is displaced. The cue ball must have some energy that is transferred to the tube ball. The cue must have some energy of motion as it is traveling across the table. During the 18th century or 1700s, the energy of motion was renamed to kinetic energy. A video from physics demos is linked on the course webpage. The kinetic energy has two definitions, one classical and two relativistic. The relativistic definition only pertains to objects moving near the speed of light which we are not investigating here. We'll stick with the classical definition. Kinetic energy. The kinetic energy, k, of a particle, is one half the product of the particle's mass, m, and the square of its speed, v. We extend this definition to any system of particles by adding up the kinetic energies of all the constituent particles to get k sub i equals one half m sub i v sub i squared for a single particle i. For a system of particles, k equals the sum from i equals one to n of one half m sub i v sub i squared. Recall from Newton's second law and momentum, we represented Newton's second law in a different form using the momentum vector p equals m vector v. We can do the same here using the magnitude p equals the square root of vector p dot vector p equals m v, where the kinetic energy becomes k equals one half m times the quantity p over m squared, which equals p squared over two m, which is sometimes more convenient to use. The units of kinetic energy are mass times speed squared, or kilogram meters squared per second squared. The units of work are Newton meters, which are also kilogram meters squared per second squared, or joules. Work and kinetic energy have the same units because they are different forms of the same more general physical property. Because velocity is a relative quantity, the kinetic energy must depend on your frame of reference. A frame of reference is chosen to simplify your calculations and subsequent analysis. One frame of reference is external to the system, that is, where the observations are made. Another frame lies attached to or moves with the system as an internal frame. Checkpoint. The equations for relative motion provide a link to calculating the kinetic energy of an object with respect to different frames of reference. For example, k equals 1.5 m times the quantity, v sub a, plus or minus v sub b squared. Represents the kinetic energy of an object with speed v sub a, that is moving relative to another object v sub b. Depending on the relative direction of motion, we can deter in whether there is a plus or minus. Example problem. Kinetic energy of an object. The problem. A. What is the kinetic energy of an 80 kg athlete running at 10 m per second? B. The Chick-Chill-Up crater in Yucatan, one of the largest existing impact craters on Earth, is thought to have been created by an asteroid traveling at 22 km per second, and releasing 4.2 times 10 to the 23 joules of kinetic energy on impact. What was its mass? C. In nuclear reactors, thermal neutrons, traveling at about 2.2 km per second, play an important role. What is the kinetic energy of such a particle? The worked solution follows. The model. Each object is treated as a point mass moving at a non-relativistic speed, so the classical expression for kinetic energy applies. Kinetic energy depends only on mass and speed, not on the direction of motion. Unit conversions are made only when needed, so that the quantities in a calculation use compatible units. The math. For an object of mass m moving at speed v, the classical kinetic energy is defined as k equals 1 half m times v squared. A. The athlete has mass m equals 80 kg and speed v equals 10 m per second. The athlete's kinetic energy follows by evaluating the kinetic energy expression. k equals 1 half times the quantity 80 kg times 10 m per second squared equals 4,000 joules. v. The asteroid's kinetic energy and speed are given, so the kinetic energy expression is solved for mass. The speed 22 km per second is 2.2 times 10 to the 4th meters per second. m equals 2k over v squared equals 2 times 4.2 times 10 to the 23rd joules over 2.2 times 10 to the 4th meters per second squared. equals 1.7 times 10 to the 15th kilograms. See, the thermal neutron has a mass m equals 1.68 times 10 to the negative 27th kilograms and speed v equals 2.2 km per second equals 2,200 meters per second. The neutron's kinetic energy follows from the same kinetic energy expression. k equals 1 half times the quantity 1.68 times 10 to the negative 27th kilograms times 22,200 meters per second squared. equals 4.1 times 10 to the negative 21st joules. The conclusion. Using the definition of kinetic energy, the athlete has 4,000 joules of kinetic energy. The chick-solubed impactor had a mass of approximately 1.7 times 10 to the 15th kilograms and the thermal neutron has 4.1 times 10 to the negative 21st joules of kinetic energy. These results show how the same expression applies across every day, planetary, and subatomic scales. They also reinforce the quadratic dependence of kinetic energy on speed, which is why high speed impacts can involve enormous energies. Example problem. Kinetic energy relative to different frames. The problem. A 75 kilograms person walks down the central aisle of a subway car at a speed of 1.5 meters per second relative to the car, whereas the train is moving at 15 meters per second relative to the tracks. A. What is the person's kinetic energy relative to the car? B. What is the person's kinetic energy relative to the tracks? C. What is the person's kinetic energy relative to a frame moving with the person? The work solution follows. The model. The person is treated as a point mass moving at non-relativistic speeds so the classical kinetic energy expression applies. Motion is along one horizontal line so velocities can be added or subtracted as signed one-dimensional quantities. Each frame measures a different speed for the same person and the kinetic energy in that frame is computed using the speed measured in that frame. The math. For an object of mass M moving at speed V in a chosen frame, the kinetic energy in that frame is K equals 1.5 M V squared. A. Relative to the subway car, the person moves at V equals 1.5 meters per second. The kinetic energy in the car frame follows from this speed. K equals 1.5 times the quantity 75 kilograms times 1.5 meters per second squared equals 84.4 joules. B. Relative to the tracks, the person's speed depends on whether the person walks in the same direction as the train or opposite the train. The velocities add for walking toward the front of the car and subtract for walking toward the back of the car. For walking toward the front of the car, the kinetic energy is K equals 1.5 times the quantity 75 kilograms times 16.5 meters per second squared equals 1.02 times 10 to the 4 joules. For walking toward the back of the car, the kinetic energy is K equals 1.5 times the quantity 75 kilograms times 13.5 meters per second squared equals 6.830 joules. C. In a frame moving with the person, the person's speed is 0. Since kinetic energy depends on speed squared, the kinetic energy depends on the speed measured in that frame. The kinetic energy in the person's own frame is K equals 0 joules. The conclusion. The person's kinetic energy is 84.4 joules relative to the subway car. 1.02 times 10 to the 4 joules relative to the tracks when walking toward the front of the car. 6.830 joules relative to the tracks when walking toward the back of the car. And 0 joules in the person's own frame. These different values occur because kinetic energy depends on the speed measured in a particular frame. This reinforces the earlier point that kinetic energy is frame dependent even though the same equation is used in each frame.
